title: Ash Wednesday (Genesis 3:19)
hookLine: ashes on the forehead: dust thou art, and into dust thou shalt return

lines: YOU'VE GOT SOMETHING ON YOUR FACE.
cards: One Wednesday in late winter, people around town have a dark smudge on their foreheads. The barista. A nurse on her lunch break.
A guy on the subway. Someone at work leans over: you've got something on your face. They know.
It's on purpose. Catholics aren't required to go to Mass that day, and still the lines form, to hear something people spend a lot of effort not thinking about. Today: Ash Wednesday.

teach.b: Ash Wednesday is the first day of Lent, the season that leads to Easter.
The ashes traditionally come from burning the palm branches of the previous year's Palm Sunday, so last spring's celebration becomes this spring's dust.
The priest, deacon or minister dips a thumb in the ashes, traces a cross on each forehead, and says one of two sentences.
One is from the Gospel of Mark: "repent, and believe the gospel." The other, the traditional one, comes from Genesis, when God speaks to Adam after the fall.
In the Douay-Rheims: "for dust thou art, and into dust thou shalt return." In the old Latin: Memento, homo, quia pulvis es, et in pulverem reverteris. Remember, man, that you are dust.
That sounds grim at first. But in Genesis, God forms the first human out of the dust of the ground and breathes life into him. Dust isn't an insult.
It's what people are made of, and what God chose to breathe into. So, as Catholics read it, the ashes say two things at once. You are going to die.
And, in the Genesis story, you are dust that God shaped by hand and filled with breath. Dust, and loved.
Catholics between eighteen and fifty-nine fast that day, one full meal and two small ones, and everyone fourteen and older skips meat.
The day isn't morbid. It's honest. Life is short, and knowing it plainly can make you kinder, braver, less hurried about things that don't matter.
Other Christians keep it too: Anglicans, Lutherans, Methodists and more.

how: On Ash Wednesday Catholics go to church to receive a cross of ashes on the forehead, often wearing it through the day, and those old enough fast and abstain from meat.

o: a day to mourn and pray for the dead
the Wednesday right before Easter Sunday
the first day of Lent, marked with ashes

it isn't a holy day of obligation, though the lines still form.

games.q: you're the priest with ashes on your thumb. the next person steps up. what do you say?
o: remember that you are dust, and to dust you shall return.
games.why: one of two sentences: remember you are dust, from Genesis 3:19, or repent and believe the gospel, from Mark 1:15.

practice: Touch your forehead lightly with your thumb, where the ashes would go, and let yourself think it: one day, I'll die; don't rush past it, and don't spiral. Then feel your breath going in and out, the breath Genesis says God gave.
If you pray, say dust, and loved; if you don't, let the plain fact make the next hour a little gentler.

wordCard.voice: Ash Wednesday. The first day of Lent, a cross of ashes on the forehead, and the words: dust thou art. Today's word.

orig.note: Hebrew, Genesis 3:19: for dust you are, and to dust you shall return. Afar is dust, the stuff Adam was shaped from.

carryVoice: Your line: dust, and loved. Both are true at once, ashes and breath. See you tomorrow.
